title: Devin MCP Server: Setup and Security Guide (2026)
summary: Devin MCP lets the Devin agent connect to external tools via the Model Context Protocol. You can set it up and manage how access is granted to each tool.
body_markdown:
## Stage-by-stage Devin MCP setup walkthrough


Getting from an empty settings page to one working connection takes four stages, and each stage ends with a decision about what the agent may touch. Stop after the third if one server covers your need.


### Stage 1: Open the MCP settings and pick a server


Go to Settings, then MCP Marketplace, and choose a single server whose data you can afford to expose. Pick the one with the narrowest job, such as a spreadsheet or a ticket queue, not the broadest.


Enable a connector and you have added a new liability line. The admin list of available integrations shows this clearly: each row has a checkbox, and the screenshot below has two connectors switched on and one off.


The agent reaches whatever you tick, so tick as little as the task requires.


*(screenshot: available connectors with enable toggles)*


With one server chosen, the next step's to give it access.


### Stage 2: Add credentials and test the connection


Select the server and enter its credentials in the auth fields. Use a key created only for this agent, with the least permission the server allows. Don't paste a personal login, because you couldn't revoke it without cutting off a person.


Then run the connection test. A passing test proves the credential's valid, not that it's narrow. Check what the key can do in the vendor's own console before you rely on it.


*(screenshot: successful test result)*


### Stage 3: Run one small read-only task


Ask the agent for something that only reads: list the last few records, or summarize one document. Compare the answer with the source system.


This is your evidence that the connection works and that it returns what you expect. If the agent reaches data you didn't intend, revoke the key and narrow the scope before anything is added. Write actions wait until a read-only run has been reviewed.


### Stage 4: Add a custom server only if needed


If the marketplace lacks the system you need, use the option to add your own server. The form asks for a server name, a transport, a command or URL, and any auth values.


Choose the transport your server supports. A local server takes a command to launch it. A hosted one takes a URL. Name the server for what it touches, so a reviewer reading the list later can tell its purpose without opening it.


Because a custom server's code is code you chose to trust, treat it as unreviewed until someone has read what it can do.


If Devin has to reach an internal tool that has no connector,[Activepieces](https://www.activepieces.com/) runs as an MCP server per project, and its flows can be exposed to Devin as tools, so the internal system can be reached through a flow; a missing integration can also be generated with AI and added privately to your own instance, a side option and not something Devin requires.


Every one of its 750 integrations, counted in the open source packages/integrations/community directory, is registered once and then runs as a step in a flow and as a tool on the project's MCP server, so there is no second catalog to publish to and nothing to wire up twice.


Record the owner, the key it uses and the date it was added, then repeat Stage 3 against it before you widen anything else.
